title: Give away one small result, not a miniature company.
summary: The free thing should finish one useful job and point naturally toward the larger problem you could solve.
why: A broad life-coaching promise is hard to try and harder to judge. A narrow output makes the value visible before asking for trust.
action: Pick one buyer situation and write the output someone can finish in one sitting. Test a manual version before software.
metric: Track useful outputs completed, not downloads alone. Record what people do next.
rule: If people collect it but never use it, shrink the job or improve the fit before adding features.
application: Hypothesis: a short decision worksheet that ends in one real-world test could lead to a supported decision sprint. This is one option, not the chosen product.
example: Paul Graham describes Stripe founders setting up users directly and Airbnb founders visiting hosts. Early manual work can uncover what must later become software. The official $100M Leads resource page lists lead magnets and first-client materials; the landing-page titles alone do not establish a detailed lesson.

title: Choose a channel where the problem already appears.
summary: Distribution starts with a specific person in a specific situation, not with a list of every marketing channel.
why: A channel that produces attention from the wrong audience makes the later funnel look broken.
action: Compare a warm introduction, a relevant community and useful public content. Choose one for a small first test. Respect community rules and consent.
metric: For each channel: qualified visits → starts → useful completions → conversations. Keep the counts separate.
rule: If a channel gets clicks but no useful completions, inspect buyer fit and promise before buying more traffic.
application: Hypothesis: reach people near a real decision deadline through an existing trusted group. Do not assume followers or a mailing list already exist.
example: Stripe separates low-touch software sold through product/marketing from high-touch software supported by human selling. The channel and price have to pay for the chosen motion. Hormozi’s branding talk adds a useful distinction: reach makes people aware; repeated pairings shape what they associate with you. He uses Nike and athletes as an illustration.

title: Make free a bounded business decision.
summary: A free worksheet, a time-limited trial and a permanent free product are different offers with different costs.
why: Unlimited free coaching can attract demand you cannot afford to serve. Free must have a job in the business.
action: Choose what is free, for whom, for how long, the usage cap and the path to paid. State the boundary before signup.
metric: Cost per useful free completion; support minutes; proportion reaching the next value event.
rule: If free value is expensive and rarely leads to a useful next step, cap usage or test a trial or paid pilot instead.
application: Hypothesis: offer one self-serve diagnostic free; test human support as a paid pilot. No price is selected.
example: Stripe pricing guidance distinguishes the underlying product from its packaging and warns against unlimited plans. That is guidance, not a rule that freemium always loses.

title: Decide what would disprove the offer before you launch it.
summary: A free offer tests usefulness and distribution. It does not prove willingness to pay.
why: People can praise a free tool without having a problem worth paying to solve.
action: Write one falsifiable prediction, recruit a small relevant group and observe use. Agree a decision date rather than collecting feedback forever.
metric: Use raw counts with denominators and interview notes. Small samples are directional, not statistical certainty.
rule: If the promised output does not help anyone act, change the job before polishing the landing page.
application: Hypothesis: watch whether a user takes the next agreed action after a decision worksheet, not whether they say the worksheet is impressive.
example: The first-users examples in Paul Graham are about direct learning and service. They do not establish a universal conversion benchmark.

title: Define passive so you can tell who is actually stuck.
summary: A follower, an email subscriber, a signup and an unused free account are different states. Choose your own event definition.
why: Without definitions, growth can be a pile of signups while nobody gets a result.
action: Write passive = a specific consented entry event, with no first-value event yet. Separate anonymous visitors from identified accounts.
metric: Passive users by channel and age since entry. Do not mix new arrivals with old inactive accounts.
rule: If you cannot identify the transition event, instrument it before claiming the funnel improved.
application: Hypothesis: passive means someone saved a decision tool but has not completed a useful next-action plan. This needs testing for the actual product.
example: Amplitude treats activation as discovering and experiencing product value, which is different from a registration event.

title: The invitation should promise the next result, not more content.
summary: A useful prompt tells someone what they will finish and how much work it takes.
why: An account welcome email is not a reason to return. The user needs a reason tied to their own job.
action: Show one concrete next step, a worked example and a clear way to start. Ask permission for reminders; do not manufacture urgency.
metric: Entry → first task started; started → completed; where people stop.
rule: If people start but stall, remove work or explain the payoff. If they never start, revisit the promise and audience.
application: Hypothesis: ask a person to choose one decision they need to make, then show what a finished action plan looks like.
example: Stripe pricing examples stress continuing the sales message and reducing decision fatigue. We apply that principle here to onboarding, not as a measured result.

title: A human-assisted first run can reveal the software you need.
summary: Do the work alongside early users before automating the wrong sequence.
why: Automation saves the most time when the workflow is known. Until then it can hide why a user struggles.
action: Observe several first runs. Note questions, manual interventions, missing inputs and unsafe outputs. Build only the repeated bottleneck.
metric: Minutes to first useful result; interventions per user; repeated friction points.
rule: If every user needs a different service, narrow the job before writing a generalized platform.
application: Hypothesis: manually help a person complete one decision sprint. Separate what required human judgment from what a form or workflow can do.
example: Paul Graham describes founders manually recruiting and delighting early users, including the Collisons doing installation themselves.

title: Measure the whole handoff, including silence.
summary: A signup can fail because of fit, effort, confusion, timing or missing trust. These need different fixes.
why: More reminders will not fix a product that asks for too much sensitive information before delivering value.
action: Ask a few non-starters what happened. Review the actual first-run experience before inventing an engagement campaign.
metric: Time to first value, abandonment step, and reasons for not continuing.
rule: If trust is the blocker, show limits, privacy and examples. If effort is the blocker, shorten the path.
application: Hypothesis: let users try a non-sensitive example before asking for a personal life history.
example: This is an original diagnostic built from activation guidance and early-user observation principles, not a Hormozi quotation.

title: Activation means a useful action happened.
summary: Define a first-value event tied to the job. Merely opening the app or chatting is not enough.
why: If the core job is making progress on a decision, the product must connect advice to an action outside the chat.
action: Draft one activation event and verify it with observed users. Then check whether activated users return more often than others.
metric: Activated users / eligible new users, within an explicitly named window. Compare by cohort and channel.
rule: If activation does not predict later value, change the definition. A correlation is a clue, not proof that forcing the event causes retention.
application: Hypothesis: activation could be a completed action plan plus one attempted real-world step. The right event is still unknown.
example: Amplitude Compass investigates actions associated with later retention. It helps find candidate aha moments; it does not establish causation by itself.

title: Shorten the path to value before adding a feature.
summary: The smallest helpful product is often a complete narrow workflow rather than a shallow version of a huge platform.
why: Every extra question, screen or permission is work before the user knows the product helps.
action: Remove one step between arrival and the useful event. Keep safety and necessary consent. Compare the next cohort, not just time-on-site.
metric: Median time to first value; completion count; quality of the output.
rule: If speed increases but output quality drops, restore the step or redesign it. Fast bad advice is not activation.
application: Hypothesis: start with one decision route, not a full catalogue of coaching, learning and opportunities.
example: Original application of the activation and first-user sources. No source establishes a particular feature roadmap for this venture.

title: Separate motivation from a product that reliably works.
summary: Software adds a quality obligation: the same promise must work when the founder is not there.
why: A compelling pitch can sell a first session. It cannot repair lost work, misleading recommendations or broken access.
action: List the failures that would destroy trust. Add basic error handling, saved work, correction routes and clear product limits before scaling.
metric: Task success; data loss incidents; support response time; human escalation rate.
rule: If the product regularly needs rescue, stop adding acquisition until the repeated failure is fixed.
application: Hypothesis: a coaching tool should say when it lacks context and make it easy to correct an inaccurate recommendation. It is not a substitute for professional care.
example: Stripe describes SaaS as an ongoing delivery relationship. The specific safety checklist is our proposed operating practice.

title: A good free experience can still be the wrong paid business.
summary: Test whether people want a continuing tool, a one-off outcome or human help. Those are different businesses.
why: A deadline-driven decision may end. Forcing a subscription onto an occasional job can create avoidable churn.
action: Offer clear alternatives in customer conversations: one-off sprint, recurring tool, assisted service. Ask for a real purchase decision only when you can deliver.
metric: Reasons for choosing a model; completed paid pilots; delivery cost. Interest is not a sale.
rule: If the need ends after one outcome, test a one-off model instead of assuming recurring software revenue.
application: Hypothesis: a decision sprint could be one-off while an ongoing team workflow could justify recurring use. Neither is chosen yet.
example: Stripe distinguishes low-touch and high-touch models and discusses pricing relative to value and sales cost.

title: Charge for a clear outcome or capability, not a vague upgrade.
summary: The paid boundary should be explainable in one sentence. More buttons are not automatically more value.
why: A customer needs to know why the paid version changes what they can accomplish.
action: Write: free helps you do X; paid helps you do Y. State scope, duration, support and cancellation plainly.
metric: Paywall exposure → checkout start → successful payment → delivered result.
rule: If users hit the boundary but do not buy, inspect value, fit, trust and price separately. Do not assume the price alone is wrong.
application: Hypothesis: paid might add a supported follow-through sprint to a free decision map. Do not promise career or income outcomes you cannot control.
example: In Stripe’s Cirtru example, the key packaging distinction is a tool versus a more managed outcome. It is a pricing critique, not proof of a revenue lift.

title: Price must support the way you sell and deliver.
summary: Self-serve software, sales-assisted software and human coaching have different costs.
why: A low monthly price with long sales calls and unlimited support may be a service business losing money in software clothing.
action: Estimate payment fees, AI/API usage, human delivery and support per customer. Use contribution after those costs to set an acquisition budget.
metric: Contribution per customer; cost to acquire a paying customer; payback period using the same time unit.
rule: If each sale adds more delivery cost than revenue, fix scope, price or delivery before adding sellers.
application: Hypothesis: price a pilot from actual delivery effort and buyer value. Use the calculator to test assumptions, not as a recommended price.
example: Stripe’s business-of-SaaS guide explains why pricing and low-/high-touch selling must fit together.

title: Use discovery to test fit before you try to close.
summary: Find the real situation, previous attempts, deadline and decision process. A no-fit customer is a useful discovery outcome.
why: Scripts help only when they surface a real buying problem. Pressure can make a sale that later turns into a refund and lost trust.
action: Ask: What are you trying to get done? Why now? What have you tried? What would a useful result look like? Who decides? Then reflect it back.
metric: Qualified conversations; fit/no-fit reasons; agreed next steps; refunds and downstream use.
rule: If there is no urgent job or credible way to help, say so. Do not invent scarcity or shame people into paying.
application: Hypothesis: demo the workflow using a buyer’s agreed non-sensitive example, then ask whether the output solves the stated job.
example: In the sales compilation, the transcript-derived 4:42–4:58 section puts the prospect ahead of the sale. In the team video he emphasizes prospect knowledge, not only product knowledge. The questions here are an adaptation, not a direct quote.

title: Treat objections as missing information before treating them as resistance.
summary: Too expensive, no time and need to think can mean several things. Diagnose rather than recite a comeback.
why: A buyer who does not understand the commitment needs clarity. A buyer who cannot afford it needs a safe no, not financing pressure.
action: Ask what specifically makes the purchase hard. Show relevant evidence or limits. Offer a smaller appropriate scope only if it still helps.
metric: Objection categories; resolution; later activation and refunds, not close rate alone.
rule: If the concern is real product weakness, fix it. If it is poor fit, disqualify.
application: Hypothesis: if someone asks how this differs from a general chatbot, show the concrete workflow, continuity and evidence rather than making broad AI claims.
example: At transcript-derived 25:01–25:30 in the sales compilation, he groups concerns around time, money, fit, authority/partner and avoidance. Some later high-ticket reframing is aggressive; we retain diagnosis and an honest no, not pressure.

title: Recurring revenue must follow recurring value.
summary: Payment alone does not tell you the product remains useful. A core user repeatedly completes the important job.
why: Habitual app opening is not the goal when the user’s job happens weekly, monthly or only near a decision.
action: Define the natural cadence of the job and the event that demonstrates repeat value. Measure retention at that cadence.
metric: Cohort retention for the core value event; paid renewal; cancellations; outcomes achieved.
rule: If the job is completed and the user leaves satisfied, distinguish success from product failure. Consider one-off pricing or a new adjacent job.
application: Hypothesis: a recurring tool may support weekly follow-through. A decision sprint may legitimately end. Product research must choose.
example: Stripe treats retention and churn as central to a subscription business. Our cadence rule applies that to an episodic coaching context.

title: Cohorts tell you whether the product improves.
summary: Compare people who started together. A growing total can hide weak retention in every group.
why: New acquisition can replace churned users and make a weak product look healthy.
action: Group users by start period and channel. At a fixed age, count who repeated the core event and who renewed. Show raw denominators.
metric: Week-N value-event retention = returning cohort users / eligible cohort users. Do not mix calendar totals with cohort rates.
rule: If later cohorts improve, investigate what changed. If they worsen after broader acquisition, inspect fit.
application: Hypothesis: track a chosen weekly action event only if weekly use matches the actual customer job.
example: Amplitude’s analytics guidance and Stripe’s SaaS model support separating acquisition, activation and retention. No benchmark is asserted here.

title: Solve why people leave before building a win-back campaign.
summary: A reminder cannot fix a finished job, bad advice, a broken product or a price mismatch.
why: Each churn reason implies a different action. One retention tactic for all reasons wastes work.
action: Read a sample of cancellation and inactivity cases. Separate completed need, missing value, friction, trust, price and failed payment.
metric: Reason counts; voluntary versus payment-related churn; recovered value, not email opens.
rule: If failure is involuntary payment loss, improve billing recovery. If the job is complete, change model or accept the exit.
application: Hypothesis: do not shame a coaching user for leaving. Make cancellation clear, preserve their work and offer re-entry when the job returns.
example: The reason-based decision tree is original applied guidance. Stripe supplies the underlying subscription model, not these precise categories.

title: Scale the narrow loop that already works.
summary: Repeat the working buyer → value → payment → return loop before adding channels, features and people together.
why: Changing everything at once makes it impossible to know what produced the result.
action: Increase one dimension at a time and watch quality, support and contribution. Add a person only to a named recurring bottleneck.
metric: Channel-level paid cohorts; contribution; support burden; delivery quality.
rule: If growth breaks quality or economics, reduce the load and fix the limiting rail before spending more.
application: Hypothesis: keep a small core workflow stable while testing one new acquisition channel. This is a proposed experiment, not a growth promise.
example: Paul Graham supports learning manually early; Stripe supplies the economic constraints. Neither guarantees speed or scale.
